claims.text: What a ROS is: an inventory of body systems, taken through a series of questions, to identify signs or symptoms the patient has now or has had.
claims.quote: A ROS is an inventory of body systems obtained through a series of questions seeking to identify signs and/or symptoms that the patient may be experiencing or has experienced.

claims.text: The systems CMS recognizes: constitutional symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss); eyes; ears, nose, mouth and throat; cardiovascular; respiratory; gastrointestinal; genitourinary; musculoskeletal; integumentary (skin and/or breast); neurological; psychiatric; endocrine; hematologic/lymphatic; allergic/immunologic.
claims.quote: For purposes of ROS, the following systems are recognized: Constitutional Symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss) Eyes Ears, Nose, Mouth, and Throat Cardiovascular Respiratory Gastrointestinal Genitourinary Musculoskeletal Integumentary (skin and/or breast) Neurological Psychiatric Endocrine Hematologic/Lymphatic Allergic/Immunologic

claims.text: Problem-pertinent ROS: ask about the system directly related to the problem(s) in the HPI, and document the patient's positive responses and pertinent negatives for that system.
claims.quote: A problem pertinent ROS inquires about the system directly related to the problem(s) identified in the HPI. DG: The patient's positive responses and pertinent negatives for the system related to the problem should be documented.

claims.text: Extended ROS: the problem's system plus a limited number of additional systems; document positives and pertinent negatives for two to nine systems.
claims.quote: An extended ROS inquires about the system directly related to the problem(s) identified in the HPI and a limited number of additional systems. DG: The patient's positive responses and pertinent negatives for two to nine systems should be documented.

claims.text: Complete ROS: the problem's system(s) plus all additional body systems, with at least ten systems reviewed. Document each system with positive or pertinent negative responses individually; for the rest, a note that all other systems are negative is permissible. Without that note, document at least ten systems individually.
claims.quote: A complete ROS inquires about the system(s) directly related to the problem(s) identified in the HPI, plus all additional body systems. DG: At least ten organ systems must be reviewed. Those systems with positive or pertinent negative responses must be individually documented. For the remaining systems, a notation indicating all other systems are negative is permissible. In the absence of such a notation, at least ten systems must be individually documented.

claims.text: Chief complaint: a short statement of the symptom, problem, condition, diagnosis or reason for the encounter, usually in the patient's own words. The record should clearly show it.
claims.quote: A chief complaint (CC) is a short statement that describes the symptom, problem, condition, diagnosis, or reason for the patient encounter. The CC is usually stated in the patient's own words, like the patient complains of upset stomach, aching joints, and fatigue. The medical record should clearly show the CC.

claims.text: HPI elements: location, quality, severity, duration, timing, context, modifying factors, and associated signs and symptoms.
claims.quote: It includes the following elements: location , quality , severity, duration, timing, context , modifying factors, and associated signs and symptoms.

claims.text: How much history today: E/M visits with levels include a medically appropriate history and exam, and the treating clinician decides their nature and extent. The care team may collect information, and the patient or caregiver may supply it through a portal or questionnaire that the clinician reviews. The extent of the history and exam isn't an element in choosing the visit level.
claims.quote: When you perform E/M codes that have levels of services, they include a medically appropriate history or physical examination. The treating physician or other qualified health care professional reporting the service determines the nature and extent of the history or physical examination. The care team may collect information, and the patient or caregiver may supply information directly through an electronic health record portal or questionnaire that's reviewed by the reporting physician or other qualified health care professional. The extent of history and physical examination isn't an element in selection of the level of these E/M service codes.

claims.text: Visit level: as of January 1, 2023, most E/M visit families are leveled by the level of medical decision making (MDM) or by the time you spend with the patient.
claims.quote: As of January 1, 2023, for most E/M visit families, choose the visit level based on the level of MDM or the amount of time you spend with the patient
